posts.title: How to brush your teeth properly
posts.metaTitle: How to Brush Your Teeth Properly | Expressions Dental
posts.metaDescription: A dentist-style guide to brushing: the right technique, how long, how often, and the spots most people miss.
posts.excerpt: Most of us brush every day, but few of us were ever shown how. A few small changes make a big difference to your teeth and gums.

sections.heading: Why technique matters
paragraphs: Plaque is a soft, sticky film of bacteria that forms on teeth every day. Left in place it causes cavities and gum disease, and within a few days it can harden into tartar, which only a professional clean can remove.
Brushing well removes plaque before it does damage. Brushing hard does not: it wears enamel and pushes gums back.

sections.heading: The basics
list: Brush twice a day, including last thing at night.
Use a soft-bristled brush with a small head.
Use a pea-sized amount of fluoride toothpaste.
Spend about two minutes each time.

sections.heading: Step by step
list: Angle the bristles about 45° towards the gum line.
Use gentle, short strokes or small circles, a couple of teeth at a time.
Work around the mouth in order: outer surfaces, inner surfaces, then chewing surfaces.
Tilt the brush upright to clean behind the front teeth, top and bottom.
Finish by gently brushing your tongue to freshen your breath.

sections.heading: Spots people often miss
paragraphs: The inner surfaces of the lower front teeth, the backs of the last molars and the gum line are where plaque and tartar build up most. Give them a little extra attention.

sections.heading: After you brush
paragraphs: Spit out the toothpaste but avoid rinsing straight away with water, so the fluoride keeps working. Clean between your teeth once a day with floss or interdental brushes, and replace your toothbrush every three months or sooner if the bristles splay.

posts.title: How to choose the right toothbrush
posts.metaTitle: How to Choose the Right Toothbrush | Expressions Dental
posts.metaDescription: Soft or medium? Manual or electric? How to pick a toothbrush that cleans well without harming your gums.
posts.excerpt: The best toothbrush is the one you use well, twice a day. Here's what to look for when you're standing in front of the shelf.

sections.heading: Choose soft bristles
paragraphs: Soft bristles remove plaque effectively and are kind to gums and enamel. Hard bristles can make gums recede over time and leave teeth sensitive, especially if you brush firmly.

sections.heading: Pick a small head and a comfortable handle
paragraphs: A smaller head reaches the back teeth more easily. The handle should feel comfortable in your hand, because a brush that is awkward to hold leads to rushed brushing.

sections.heading: Manual or electric?
paragraphs: Both work well when used properly. Electric brushes can help people who find it hard to brush thoroughly, such as people with arthritis, children or anyone wearing braces. A manual brush used with good technique is just as effective for most people.

sections.heading: Extras worth considering
list: A tongue cleaner on the back of the head, if bad breath is a concern.
Interdental brushes for gaps, bridges or braces.
A child-sized brush with a chunky handle for young children.

sections.heading: When to replace it
paragraphs: Replace your brush every three months, or sooner if the bristles splay or after an illness. Splayed bristles clean far less well.

posts.title: Mouth cancer: signs to watch for and how to lower your risk
posts.metaTitle: Mouth Cancer: Signs, Symptoms and Risk Factors | Expressions
posts.metaDescription: Know the early signs of mouth cancer, what increases your risk, and why regular dental check-ups help catch problems early.
posts.excerpt: Mouth cancer is much easier to treat when it is found early. Knowing the warning signs, and having regular check-ups, makes a real difference.

sections.heading: Signs to watch for
paragraphs: Mouth cancer can affect the lips, tongue, cheeks, gums, floor or roof of the mouth. See a dentist or doctor if any of these lasts more than two weeks:
list: A mouth ulcer or sore that does not heal
A red or white patch inside the mouth
A lump or thickening in the mouth, lip or neck
Pain or difficulty chewing or swallowing
A loose tooth with no obvious cause, or dentures that suddenly stop fitting

sections.heading: What increases the risk
list: Smoking, and chewing tobacco, gutka, paan or areca nut
Drinking alcohol, especially together with tobacco
Infection with certain types of human papillomavirus (HPV)
Too much sun on the lips

sections.heading: Lowering your risk
paragraphs: Stopping tobacco in every form is the single most important step, and it is never too late to benefit. Keep alcohol within recommended limits, eat plenty of fruit and vegetables, and protect your lips from the sun.

sections.heading: Why check-ups matter
paragraphs: At a routine check-up your dentist looks at the whole mouth, not just the teeth. Many changes are harmless, but anything unusual can be referred for tests early, when treatment is most likely to succeed.
